paragraphs: FANOVA models describe a function through components associated with individual variables and their interactions. This paper develops a Bayesian framework for deciding which components matter and estimating them. The aim is to represent complex relationships while retaining an interpretable account of how different variables contribute.

The framework allows different amounts of sparsity across interaction orders, within an order, and among covariates. In plain language, it can accommodate situations where only some variables or interactions are useful, without requiring every part of the decomposition to follow the same pattern. The authors also provide tuning and implementation guidance intended to improve the scalability of learning and prediction.

A central contribution is expressing several deterministic and Bayesian nonparametric approaches within one formulation. This makes their relationships easier to compare and supplies Bayesian counterparts that support uncertainty quantification. The framework also suggests additional model designs: the paper introduces a Dirichlet mixing model intended to address limitations of existing approaches. Its contribution is therefore both a modeling framework and a way to organize and extend earlier methods.
icml-2024-a-unified-view-of-fanova-a-com.tldr: A unified Bayesian FANOVA framework supports flexible component selection, uncertainty quantification, and connections among existing modeling approaches.

paragraphs: Deep kernel learning combines neural networks’ ability to learn representations with Gaussian processes’ uncertainty estimates. Training this combination can nevertheless lead to overfitting. The paper focuses on a particular failure: learned kernels can connect observations through spurious correlations, producing relationships that the model should not rely on.

The proposed method, amortized variational deep kernel learning, uses amortized inducing points together with shared parameters between the amortization and deep kernel networks. This links two parts of the training objective: the term rewarding agreement with observations and the term controlling model capacity. According to the authors, that dependency prevents the fit term from dominating optimization and creating the unwanted correlations.

Experiments cover tabular data, graph node classification, and image classification. The method consistently outperforms conventional deep kernel learning and standard Gaussian processes on the reported tabular tasks. It also improves node classification accuracy over deep kernel learning and improves both accuracy and negative log-likelihood on CIFAR100. These findings support the proposed training design across the evaluated settings.
icml-2024-amortized-variational-deep-ker.tldr: Sharing parameters between inducing-point amortization and deep kernel learning helps prevent spurious correlations and improves results across several evaluated tasks.

paragraphs: Scientific classification can involve a mechanistic model of how observations arise, alongside hidden nuisance parameters that affect those observations. This paper addresses situations where the distribution of both labels and nuisance parameters changes between training and deployment. The authors call this generalized label shift and explain that direct classification can then produce biased predictions and invalid uncertainty estimates.

Their approach treats classification as hypothesis testing in the presence of nuisance parameters. It estimates how a classifier’s true-positive and false-positive behavior varies across the entire nuisance parameter space. That information is used to construct decision cutoffs that remain invariant under the specified distributional shift.

The method equips a pretrained classifier with adaptation capabilities and produces prediction sets with valid uncertainty while maintaining high statistical power. Its value is that uncertainty assessment explicitly accounts for the nuisance variation responsible for the shift. The authors demonstrate the approach on biology and astroparticle physics problems using data from realistic mechanistic models, connecting the statistical construction to scientific classification tasks.
icml-2024-classification-under-nuisance-.tldr: A hypothesis-testing approach gives pretrained classifiers valid prediction sets under shifts in both labels and latent nuisance parameters.

paragraphs: Optimization on curved spaces requires algorithms and guarantees that account for geometry. This paper studies Riemannian gradient descent and Riemannian proximal point methods for geodesically convex problems. It quantifies their convergence rates and develops variants offering different trade-offs, including versions where proximal steps are computed only approximately.

A central result establishes that the iterates remain within a ball around an optimizer. The radius depends on the starting distance and, in some cases, the space’s curvature. Earlier analyses assumed bounded iterates without fully quantifying that bound. Establishing it directly makes the resulting convergence statements more complete and clarifies how initialization and geometry enter the analysis.

The paper also gives an implementable inexact proximal algorithm and establishes several properties of proximal methods in this setting. They can operate in the presence of positive curvature, and the proximal operator does not increase distance from any optimizer. The authors additionally quantify the smoothness of the associated Moreau envelope and conduct empirical tests beyond the scope of their theory.
icml-2024-convergence-and-trade-offs-in-.tldr: New analyses quantify convergence on curved spaces by proving bounded iterates and establishing practical and geometric properties of proximal methods.

paragraphs: Open-ended reinforcement learning needs environments that are challenging enough to demand extended learning but fast enough to support experimentation. The authors argue that existing benchmarks often compromise one of these requirements. They introduce Craftax-Classic, a JAX rewrite of Crafter, and Craftax, a more demanding environment built by extending the underlying mechanics.

Craftax-Classic runs up to 250 times faster than the original Python implementation. The reported PPO run completes one billion environment interactions in under an hour on a single GPU and averages 90% of optimal reward. These results demonstrate the computational accessibility of the rewritten environment and motivate adding a harder benchmark.

The main Craftax environment incorporates elements inspired by NetHack and requires exploration, long-term planning, memory, and adaptation as new parts of the world appear. In the reported evaluations, methods using global exploration, episodic exploration, or unsupervised environment design fail to make material progress. The authors therefore position Craftax as a way to investigate difficult open-ended learning with limited computational resources.
icml-2024-craftax-a-lightning-fast-bench.tldr: Craftax combines fast simulation with a challenging open-ended environment that tested exploration and environment-design methods struggle to solve.

paragraphs: This paper asks whether a neural network’s internal weights can be recovered by observing its input-output behavior. Several symmetries make this difficult: neurons can be permuted, networks can be overparameterized, and activation functions introduce additional equivalences. The authors show that each neuron’s incoming weight vector is identifiable up to a sign or scaling ambiguity, depending on the activation function.

Expand-and-Cluster turns that result into a two-step recovery method. First, multiple oversized student networks are trained to imitate the target network. This expansion relaxes the nonconvex optimization problem. A tailored clustering procedure then finds weight vectors shared across the trained students, identifying those shared vectors with the target network’s weights.

The method is designed to recover both layer sizes and weights for commonly used activation functions. The authors demonstrate recovery for trained shallow and deep networks with less than 10% layer-size overhead. They also analyze 150 synthetic problems to characterize an axis of recovery difficulty. Together, these results examine both what can be identified and how difficult identification is in practice.
icml-2024-expand-and-cluster-parameter-r.tldr: Training oversized imitators and clustering their shared weights can recover network sizes and weights, subject to activation-dependent sign or scaling ambiguities.

paragraphs: Forecasting measurements from connected sensors requires learning relationships across both locations and time. Graph neural networks can represent these relationships, but many forecasting methods assume that all inputs are available. This paper addresses the harder case where missing observations obscure the spatial and temporal patterns needed to predict future measurements.

The method progressively coarsens the input series along both dimensions. This produces a hierarchy of representations that capture dynamics at different spatial and temporal scales. An interpretable attention mechanism then combines those representations using both the available measurements and the pattern of missing data. Missingness therefore helps determine which representations contribute to a forecast.

On synthetic and real-world benchmarks, the approach outperforms the compared state-of-the-art methods under several missing-data distributions. The reported advantage is especially pronounced when observations disappear in contiguous blocks. The findings support using multiple resolutions to forecast through gaps, with attention adapting the combination of resolutions to what was observed and where information is absent.
icml-2024-graph-based-forecasting-with-m.tldr: Combining spatial and temporal resolutions with missingness-aware attention improves graph forecasting, particularly when observations are absent in contiguous blocks.

paragraphs: Regression algorithms often optimize a surrogate loss rather than the squared error ultimately of interest. This paper studies when success on the surrogate supports success on squared loss within a specified hypothesis class. Such H-consistency bounds connect the training objective to the intended prediction objective while accounting for the functions the learner can actually use.

The authors first extend the general tools needed to establish these bounds. Under a symmetric-distribution assumption and a bounded hypothesis set, they obtain positive results for Huber loss, all lp losses with p at least one, and squared epsilon-insensitive loss. They also obtain a negative result for the epsilon-insensitive loss used in Support Vector Regression. Thus, the analysis distinguishes two closely related insensitive losses.

The paper then applies this reasoning to adversarial regression, deriving principled surrogate objectives and corresponding learning algorithms. Experiments report favorable results for those algorithms. The theoretical contribution is conditional on the stated assumptions, while the experiments provide evidence for the usefulness of objectives developed from that analysis.
icml-2024-h-consistency-guarantees-for-r.tldr: Under symmetry and boundedness assumptions, new H-consistency results distinguish regression surrogates and motivate algorithms for adversarial regression.

paragraphs: World-model reinforcement learning uses learned predictions of the environment to train an agent through imagined experience. Its usefulness depends on accurate predictions, effective exploration, and manageable computation. HIEROS addresses these concerns with a hierarchical policy that learns representations at different temporal scales and imagines trajectories within a latent space.

The world model uses S5 layers, which support parallel prediction during training and iterative prediction during interaction and imagination. This combination matters because learning from sequences and generating future steps have different computational needs. The authors report more efficient training than recurrent-network world models and more efficient imagination than Transformer-based world models.

The hierarchy allows imagined behavior to be considered at multiple time scales, alongside the sequence model’s computational design. On Atari 100k, HIEROS exceeds the reported state of the art in both mean and median normalized human score. The authors also report accurate prediction of complex dynamics and stronger exploration than existing approaches. These findings support the combined architecture in the evaluated reinforcement-learning setting.
icml-2024-hieros-hierarchical-imaginatio.tldr: HIEROS combines hierarchical imagination with an S5 world model to improve computational efficiency, exploration, and reported Atari 100k performance.

paragraphs: Bayesian optimization uses probabilistic models to choose promising evaluations of a black-box objective. Some objectives have a composite structure: an input first produces an intermediate output, which then determines the final result. When evaluations reveal both outputs, the intermediate information can help guide the search. Existing approaches struggle when that information is high-dimensional.

Joint Composite Latent Space Bayesian Optimization, or JoCo, tackles this problem by learning compressed representations of both inputs and intermediate outputs. Neural encoders and probabilistic models are trained jointly, allowing the compression to adapt as part of the optimization framework. Bayesian optimization then operates on the resulting manageable latent representations.

The approach matters because it provides a way to use rich intermediate observations without directly handling their full dimensionality throughout the search. The authors identify generative AI, molecular design, and robotics as relevant settings for this problem structure. Across a wide range of simulated and real-world problems, JoCo outperforms the compared state-of-the-art methods for high-dimensional Bayesian optimization.
icml-2024-joint-composite-latent-space-b.tldr: JoCo jointly learns compressed inputs and intermediate outputs to make Bayesian optimization more effective on high-dimensional composite objectives.

paragraphs: Conservation laws identify quantities that remain unchanged as training dynamics evolve. Such laws are established for Euclidean gradient flows, including certain linear and ReLU networks. This paper develops a framework to characterize conservation laws in a broader setting that includes non-Euclidean geometries and dynamics with momentum.

A key result is that conservation laws for momentum dynamics depend explicitly on time. The authors also find that adding momentum often reduces the number of conserved quantities. For linear networks, their framework identifies all momentum conservation laws and shows that they are fewer than in gradient flow, except in sufficiently overparameterized regimes.

For the ReLU networks considered, no conservation law remains under momentum. A related phenomenon appears in non-Euclidean metrics used for nonnegative matrix factorization: the framework determines all conservation laws for gradient flow, yet none persists in the momentum case. These results show that changing training dynamics or geometry can fundamentally change the invariants available for analyzing learning, even when the underlying modeling setting remains closely related.
icml-2024-keep-the-momentum-conservation.tldr: A general conservation-law framework shows that momentum introduces time dependence and often removes invariants present in gradient flow.

paragraphs: This paper evaluates language models through the geographic patterns in their predictions. Geography provides a useful testing ground because many aspects of human life have measurable spatial distributions. The authors define geographic bias as systematic error in geospatial predictions and use this perspective to examine both factual knowledge and judgments about places.

The models can produce accurate zero-shot geographic ratings, with rankings reaching a Spearman correlation of 0.89 with ground truth. However, the authors also find recurring biases across objective and subjective topics. In particular, the evaluated models express unfavorable judgments about locations with lower socioeconomic conditions, including much of Africa, on sensitive topics such as attractiveness, morality, and intelligence.

These subjective ratings are model outputs, not established properties of the people living in those locations. The paper introduces a score for quantifying geographic bias and finds substantial variation among models. Its findings show that useful geographic predictive ability can coexist with harmful systematic associations, making bias measurement a distinct part of evaluating what language models say about the world.
icml-2024-large-language-models-are-geog.tldr: Language models can make accurate geographic predictions while also producing systematic negative judgments about places with lower socioeconomic conditions.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning with continuous states or actions presents difficult questions about regret: how much reward a learner loses while discovering how to act. This paper introduces a structural assumption called nu-smoothness to obtain guarantees in a broad setting. The assumption generalizes many previously studied cases, including linear and Lipschitz Markov decision processes.

Both proposed algorithms represent the decision process using an orthogonal feature map built from Legendre polynomials. This supplies a common mathematical representation for learning in the smooth setting. The two methods then offer different balances between the breadth of their assumptions and the computation required to use them.

Legendre-Eleanor achieves no regret under weaker assumptions but is computationally inefficient. Legendre-LSVI runs in polynomial time, while covering a smaller class of problems. The authors analyze both methods’ regret and report the best guarantees in their comparison with existing reinforcement-learning theory. The contribution therefore includes an explicit trade-off: broader theoretical applicability comes with greater computational difficulty, while efficient computation requires a narrower setting.
icml-2024-no-regret-reinforcement-learni.tldr: Legendre-polynomial representations yield regret guarantees for smooth MDPs, with a trade-off between weaker assumptions and computational efficiency.

paragraphs: Kernel methods often work well on observations from dynamical systems, even though such data can violate the independence assumptions common in learning theory. This paper develops a weaker basis for explaining that behavior. It introduces empirical weak convergence, an assumption allowing the data to approach a random asymptotic distribution.

The new assumption is strictly weaker than previous assumptions in the field. Under empirical weak convergence, the authors establish consistency for support vector machines, kernel mean embeddings, and empirical expectations taking values in general Hilbert spaces. The analysis therefore covers more than a single prediction method or a single type of output.

The results apply to finite-dimensional and infinite-dimensional outputs, extending classical statistical-learning arguments to the latter setting. This also makes the analysis applicable to conditional kernel mean embeddings. The significance is a larger class of dependent data-generating processes for which learning can receive theoretical support. The guarantees still rely on empirical weak convergence, providing a specified route beyond independent or mixing observations rather than a claim about arbitrary dependence.
icml-2024-on-the-consistency-of-kernel-m.tldr: Empirical weak convergence provides a weaker assumption under which several kernel methods remain consistent with dependent observations.

paragraphs: SHAP assigns contributions to features to explain an individual model prediction, but computing these scores exactly can be difficult. Previous efficient-computation results for several model families relied on independent features. That assumption simplifies the mathematics, yet it excludes dependencies that often occur in real data.

This paper studies computational complexity when the feature distribution instead has Markovian structure. Such a structure allows dependencies while imposing an organized form on them. The authors prove that exact SHAP scores can be computed in polynomial time under this assumption for weighted automata, disjoint disjunctive normal forms, and decision trees.

The result establishes an efficient-computation guarantee beyond feature independence for the specified model classes. Its importance is theoretical: dependence alone does not rule out tractable exact explanations when that dependence has the structure studied here. The guarantee concerns Markovian distributions and the named model families, so its scope is more specific than making exact SHAP computation efficient for every model or every correlated dataset.
icml-2024-on-the-tractability-of-shap-ex.tldr: Exact SHAP scores are computable in polynomial time for several model classes under Markovian feature dependence.

paragraphs: State-space models describe sequential observations through underlying hidden states. Learning their parameters and inferring those states typically requires difficult posterior calculations. Variational sequential Monte Carlo combines particle methods with variational inference to make these calculations manageable, but its standard form repeatedly processes a fixed batch of observations.

This paper develops an online version for data streams. It uses stochastic approximation to distribute estimation of the variational objective’s gradient over time. The resulting algorithm updates model parameters and adapts the particle proposal mechanism entirely as observations arrive. This brings both learning tasks into the same on-the-fly procedure.

The authors provide rigorous convergence results describing behavior as the number of observations grows without bound. Numerical illustrations also show strong convergence behavior and usefulness when processing batches. The contribution is therefore both an algorithmic extension to streaming data and a theoretical account of its long-run behavior. Its reported batch usefulness suggests that the online construction can also be valuable when observations are already available together.
icml-2024-online-variational-sequential-.tldr: Online VSMC learns state-space-model parameters and adapts particle proposals as data arrive, with asymptotic convergence guarantees.

paragraphs: Graph foundation models aim to learn from extensive, varied graph data so that their capabilities transfer across tasks and domains. This differs from training a separate graph neural network for each dataset and task. The paper identifies positive transfer as the central challenge: diversity in the training collection must become useful shared knowledge.

As a position paper, it advocates organizing development around a graph vocabulary. The proposed vocabulary consists of basic transferable units that encode invariances in graphs. Inspired by foundation models in vision and language, this perspective asks what reusable structural content can carry across otherwise different graph problems.

The authors ground vocabulary construction in network analysis, expressiveness, and stability. These provide ways to reason about graph structure, representational capability, and robustness of the resulting representations. The paper argues that this viewpoint could guide future graph foundation models in a direction compatible with neural scaling laws. That is a proposed design perspective and potential research direction, rather than a reported guarantee that a particular vocabulary produces scaling or transfer.
icml-2024-position-graph-foundation-mode.tldr: This position paper proposes a graph vocabulary of transferable invariant units to guide graph foundation-model design.

paragraphs: Contextual optimal transport learns how distributions should be connected when the connection depends on additional information. In this paper’s application, that context includes drug dosage, and the distributions describe cell types. The challenge is to predict transportation plans that change with context, potentially including contexts not encountered during learning.

The authors introduce QontOT, a quantum-computing formulation for amortized optimization of these plans. Its mathematical basis is a direct connection between doubly stochastic matrices and unitary operators. This connects the representation of transportation plans with quantum computation and supplies an alternative formulation to existing neural optimal-transport approaches.

The method is evaluated on synthetic and real data through predictions of dosage-dependent cell-type distributions. The paper also reports a 24-qubit hardware experiment on a task described as challenging for classical computers. In that experiment, performance exceeds what the authors’ classical neural optimal-transport approach achieves. The result supports this particular quantum formulation and comparison, while the authors frame the work as an initial step toward quantum prediction of contextual transportation plans.
icml-2024-quantum-theory-and-application.tldr: QontOT uses a connection between transport matrices and quantum operators to learn contextual transportation plans, with a reported 24-qubit hardware demonstration.

paragraphs: A regression system may benefit from handing a prediction to an expert instead of always answering itself. Choosing among several experts is complicated by regression’s continuous range of possible outputs. This paper develops a framework that learns when to predict and when to defer, while accounting for the costs of those decisions.

The authors analyze two training arrangements. In the single-stage case, the predictor and deferral function are learned together. In the two-stage case, a deferral function is learned for an existing pretrained predictor. Both receive new surrogate losses supported by H-consistency bounds, which provide non-asymptotic guarantees tied to the chosen hypothesis set.

The framework accommodates multiple experts, any bounded regression loss, and costs depending on either the instance or its label. Its single-stage formulation also includes a prior single-expert abstention setting as a special case. Minimizing the proposed objectives produces new deferral algorithms, and extensive experiments demonstrate their effectiveness. The contribution combines flexible decision costs with theoretical support for learning the predictor’s delegation behavior.
icml-2024-regression-with-multi-expert-d.tldr: A regression framework learns when to defer to multiple experts, with surrogate objectives backed by hypothesis-specific consistency guarantees.

paragraphs: This paper develops a way to generate samples from a target density whose normalization constant need not be known. The method begins with samples from a reference density and moves them toward the target. Its interacting particle systems require target-to-reference density ratios but do not require gradients of the target density.

The construction follows a geometric mixture connecting the reference and target densities. The authors obtain a velocity field by solving a Poisson equation, using a reproducing-kernel Hilbert-space representation to make the problem tractable. This yields a mean-field differential equation that can be discretized using finitely many particles. They also derive the equation from successive linearizations within sample-driven optimal transport.

A stochastic variant broadens the proposed approach. Empirical evaluations show high-quality samples across varied target distributions, with results exceeding comparable gradient-free particle systems and competing with gradient-based alternatives. The practical attraction is a sampling procedure based on accessible density ratios and reference samples, supported by a connection between Fisher-Rao flow, kernel representations, and transport.
icml-2024-sampling-in-unit-time-with-ker.tldr: Kernel Fisher-Rao flow produces gradient-free particle samplers using reference samples and unnormalized density ratios.

paragraphs: Unbalanced optimal transport supports comparisons between measures whose total mass need not be normalized. This paper adds explicit sparsity constraints to transportation plans. It considers both a cap on the number of nonzero entries in each column and a cap on the number across the entire plan, giving control over where transportation connections can appear.

The proposed formulations build on maximum-mean-discrepancy-based unbalanced transport. The authors show that their optimization problems are equivalent to maximizing a weakly submodular function under either uniform or partition matroid constraints. These mathematical structures express the permitted selections of nonzero entries and make the problem accessible to discrete greedy optimization.

The paper develops efficient gradient-based greedy algorithms and provides theoretical guarantees for them. Empirically, the algorithms select diverse support sets, meaning the chosen nonzero locations cover varied connections. Applications illustrate the approach’s effectiveness. The main contribution is a bridge between sparse transport design and structured discrete optimization, allowing explicit limits on the plan’s support to be incorporated into a principled algorithm.
icml-2024-submodular-framework-for-struc.tldr: Sparse unbalanced transport can be formulated as weakly submodular maximization, enabling greedy algorithms with theoretical guarantees.

paragraphs: Two approaches can make neural-network learning easier: increasing the network’s size and arranging training examples into a curriculum. The lottery ticket hypothesis motivates the first by suggesting that larger networks are more likely to contain a favorably initialized subnetwork. Curriculum learning instead tries to guide progress through the order in which examples appear.

This paper connects these ideas through a theoretical analysis of a two-layer network learning an XOR-like Gaussian mixture problem. The analysis uses an online learning setting and examines how the amount of overparameterization changes the benefits available from a curriculum. This makes network size and example ordering parts of the same learning question.

The results show that substantial overparameterization can simplify the task while reducing the additional benefit of a curriculum. This offers a theoretical explanation for why curricula may provide little improvement in deep learning. The conclusion is grounded in the analyzed network and problem setting: it identifies a mechanism by which larger models can diminish curriculum gains, rather than establishing that curricula never help.
icml-2024-tilting-the-odds-at-the-lotter.tldr: A theoretical two-layer-network analysis shows that strong overparameterization can reduce the additional benefit of curriculum learning.

paragraphs: Neural surrogate solvers can accelerate partial differential equation calculations, but many are tied to fixed domain sizes, geometries, and boundary conditions. This paper proposes SNAP-DDM, which combines specialized neural solvers with domain decomposition. The aim is to reuse accurate solvers for smaller subproblems when solving larger problems with varied layouts.

The approach uses an ensemble of specialized neural operators to solve subdomain problems containing arbitrary boundary conditions and geometric parameters. These operators are incorporated into standard domain-decomposition algorithms. The overall construction connects learned local solution capabilities with an established method for assembling solutions across a larger domain.

The authors tailor the system to two-dimensional electromagnetics and fluid-flow problems. Changes to network architecture and loss design produce specialized subdomain solvers with accuracy described as near unity. Used within domain decomposition, these solvers accurately handle freeform electromagnetics and fluid problems across a wide range of domain sizes. The findings support specialization at the subdomain level as a route toward more flexible neural PDE solving in the demonstrated settings.
icml-2024-towards-general-neural-surroga.tldr: SNAP-DDM combines specialized neural subdomain solvers with domain decomposition to solve varied two-dimensional electromagnetic and fluid problems.

paragraphs: An AI prediction gives a user an answer, while uncertainty quantification adds probabilistic information about that particular prediction. This paper investigates whether that additional information helps people make better decisions. It focuses on instance-level uncertainty, meaning uncertainty attached to an individual case, rather than only a broad description of model performance.

The researchers conduct two online behavioral experiments using uncertainty estimates calibrated with a strict scoring rule. In the first experiment, participants make better decisions when given uncertainty information alongside predictions than when given predictions alone. This provides direct experimental evidence that the additional probabilities can be useful to human decision-makers.

The second experiment examines several ways of presenting probabilistic information and finds benefits across those representations. The result suggests that the observed usefulness is not confined to a single presentation format. Together, the experiments support further use of high-quality, case-specific uncertainty in AI-assisted decisions. The authors frame the practical implication cautiously: such information may improve decisions in real systems, beyond what predictions alone provide.
icml-2024-using-ai-uncertainty-quantific.tldr: Two online experiments find that calibrated, case-specific AI uncertainty improves human decisions across several probability presentation formats.

paragraphs: Pretrained diffusion models have enabled zero-shot editing of images, and this paper explores corresponding techniques for audio. Both proposed techniques use DDPM inversion with pretrained diffusion models. The shared goal is to edit an existing audio signal using capabilities already present in the model.

The first technique, ZETA, adapts a text-based editing approach from the image domain. Text provides a way to specify the desired change. The second, ZEUS, discovers semantically meaningful editing directions without supervision. Its focus is finding modifications within the model that correspond to recognizable changes in the audio, rather than requiring a supervised description of those directions.

Applied to music, ZEUS exposes changes ranging from altering the participation of particular instruments to improvising on a melody. These examples indicate that the discovered directions can affect musically meaningful aspects of a signal. The paper’s contribution is the exploration of two complementary zero-shot routes to audio editing: describing changes through language and discovering useful changes without supervision.
icml-2024-zero-shot-unsupervised-and-tex.tldr: ZETA and ZEUS use pretrained diffusion models for zero-shot audio editing through text guidance or unsupervised discovery of meaningful changes.
